W4220703499.c001.text: If God had foreknowledge of a particular future choice, that choice cannot be free with libertarian freedom.
W4220703499.c001.quote: Hasker argues that if God had foreknowledge of a particular future choice, that choice cannot be free with libertarian freedom.

W4220703499.c002.text: Given a certain theory of time, it is possible to reconcile divine foreknowledge with libertarian freedom.
W4220703499.c002.quote: I hold, to the contrary, that, given a certain theory of time, it is possible to reconcile divine foreknowledge with libertarian freedom.

W4220703499.c003.text: Whether my interpretation of St. Anselm’s work is historically correct is irrelevant to the argument.
W4220703499.c003.quote: whether or not my interpretation of St. Anselm’s work is correct historically is not relevant to the purposes of the present paper.

W4220703499.c004.text: Our fundamental disagreement lies in what each of us takes to be required for libertarian free will.
W4220703499.c004.quote: one of the fundamental disagreements between us lies in what each of us takes to be required for libertarian free will.

W4220703499.c005.text: Within the Christian tradition human agents are held morally responsible for their actions.
W4220703499.c005.quote: A first reason is that within the Christian tradition human agents are held morally responsible for their actions.

W4220703499.c006.text: The Anselmian thesis: a created agent can choose with aseity only if he faces open options and it is up to him which option he chooses.
W4220703499.c006.quote: The Anselmian thesis is that in a universe made by God the created agent can choose with aseity only if he faces open options and it is up to him which option he chooses.

W4220703499.c007.text: The truth about, and knowledge of, a free choice depends upon that actual choice (Grounding Principle).
W4220703499.c007.quote: This entails that truth about, and knowledge of, a free choice depends upon that actual choice. I label this the “Grounding Principle”.

W4220703499.c008.text: Unobstructed power means the power is free from any external, necessitating factor that makes the choice inevitable.
W4220703499.c008.quote: ‘Unobstructed’ means (roughly) that the power is free from any external, necessitating factor that makes it inevitable that S choose one way rather than the other.

W4220703499.c009.text: If the Grounding Principle is correct, there are no Molinist “counterfactuals of freedom”.
W4220703499.c009.quote: If the Grounding Principle is correct, there simply are no Molinist “counterfactuals of freedom”.

W4220703499.c010.text: An internal necessity of the form “If X then X” does not conflict with free will.
W4220703499.c010.quote: I take it that this sort of necessity does not conflict with free will.

W4220703499.c011.text: If God knows at T1 that S will choose B at T2, then S lacks open options and power, so the choice is not free.
W4220703499.c011.quote: Hasker holds that this attempt to solve the dilemma of freedom and divine foreknowledge fails. On his understanding of “free will”, if S chooses B at T2, and if it is true at T1 that “S chooses B at T2”—as it must be if God foreknows S’s choice or if we live in an isotemporal universe—then S’s choice cannot really be free.

W4220703499.c012.text: Hasker’s PEP7 shows that, given God’s knowledge, S cannot be in power to refrain from choosing B, so S is not free at T2.
W4220703499.c012.quote: Take ‘P’ to be ‘God knows at T1 that S chooses B at T2.’ That entails ‘Q’; ‘S chooses B at T2.’ Assuming P, it cannot be in anyone’s power, including S’s, to bring it about that P is false.

W4220703499.c013.text: It is difficult to locate the time at which S could exercise the power Hasker requires, undermining Hasker’s analysis.
W4220703499.c013.quote: I find it difficult to pinpoint the time at which S might actually exercise the sort of power Hasker has in mind—the power involved in his definition of free will, that is, to choose A or to refrain from choosing A (say by choosing B).

W4220703499.c014.text: Hasker's analysis makes S unfree at the moment he actually chooses.
W4220703499.c014.quote: On Hasker’s analysis, this seems to render S unfree at the time he actually chooses.

W4220703499.c015.text: Since no one can make P false or Q false, S lacks the power required for free will at the time of his choice.
W4220703499.c015.quote: Since it is not in anyone’s power to bring it about that P is false, it is not in anyone’s power to bring it about that Q is false, and S does not have the power required for free will at the time he makes his choice.

W4220703499.c016.text: The logical necessity that if S chooses B at T2 then S chooses B at T2 is harmless and compatible with freedom.
W4220703499.c016.quote: The consequent necessity at work here seems to me innocuous vis‑à‑vis free will because it is just a logical necessity traceable to S’s own choice—if S chooses B at T2, then it cannot fail to be the case that S chooses B at T2.

W4220703499.c017.text: Hasker fails to analyze free‑will power in terms of the agent’s strength.
W4220703499.c017.quote: But Hasker does not analyze the power of free will in terms of the agent’s strength.

W4220703499.c018.text: Free‑will power must include the possibility of choosing otherwise, which makes the actual choice render the alternative impossible in a way that conflicts with freedom.
W4220703499.c018.quote: The agent’s power must include the possibility of choosing otherwise, where “possible” entails that the actual choosing by the agent makes it impossible for him to choose otherwise—impossible in a way that conflicts with free will.

W4220703499.c019.text: At T1 S cannot choose between A and B because he cannot be choosing before he is choosing.
W4220703499.c019.quote: It is not possible for S to choose between A and B at T1, since S cannot be choosing before he is choosing.

W4220703499.c020.text: According to Hasker, T2 does not exist at T1 because the future is not existent.
W4220703499.c020.quote: At T1, T2 does not exist. It does not exist on Hasker’s analysis of time in which the future is just not existent at all.

W4220703499.c021.text: Hasker’s explication of power and his understanding of free will are not intuitive.
W4220703499.c021.quote: Hasker’s explication of that power, and hence his understanding of free will, does not strike me as intuitive.

W4220703499.c022.text: Hasker’s PEPs entail that God’s knowledge conflicts with human freedom even when that knowledge depends on the agent’s free choice.
W4220703499.c022.quote: And they entail that God’s knowledge conflicts with human freedom, even if the knowledge is dependent on the agent’s free choice.

W4220703499.c023.text: On the Anselmian view, S is entirely responsible for his choice of B at T2.
W4220703499.c023.quote: On the Anselmian view, S is entirely responsible for his choice for B at T2.

W4220703499.c024.text: The PEPs are dubious and add no value to the free will of created agents.
W4220703499.c024.quote: The PEPs are intrinsically dubious, and the power they express seems to add nothing of value to the free will of the created agent.

W4220703499.c025.text: Positing God as eternal, with all time present to Him, best respects both divine foreknowledge and libertarian free will.
W4220703499.c025.quote: If the grounding principle is correct—the truth about, and knowledge of, a free choice is dependent upon the actual making of the choice itself—then positing that God is eternal, and all of time is immediately present to Him, seems the most adequate way to respect both sides of the dilemma.

W4220703499.c026.quote: Hasker, following Purtill, holds that free will requires that the agent (S) be able to change what he chooses.

objections.text: Consider Maya, a chess player at T1 who is weighing two moves, A (Nf3) and B (d4). She deliberates for ten seconds, then plays A. Her premise is that she is choosing now, while the options are open. Suppose a rival says: 'At T1 you cannot choose between A and B, since choosing is something you can only be doing after you have chosen.' Test this against Maya's case. Her deliberation is itself the process of choosing: weighing reasons, rejecting B, settling on A. Nothing in that process requires the choice to be complete before it begins. If choosing could occur only after it had finished, no one could ever deliberate toward a decision, and Maya's ten seconds would be idle. The inference treats 'is choosing' as a state that must already hold, when for a free agent it is the activity that makes the choice occur. The claim that one cannot be choosing before one is choosing is true only if 'choosing' names a completed event, which begs the question about whether T1 is open.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c019 fails because it assumes that 'choosing' is a completed state that must already obtain before deliberation can count as choosing, whereas Maya's case shows that choosing is an ongoing activity that is open at T1 and can be in progress before its outcome is settled.

objections.text: Ann knows on Tuesday that Sam will freely choose pancakes Friday. She knows this because Sam told her his intention Tuesday, and over twenty years he has never changed his mind after such announcements, though he always could. Friday arrives and Sam freely chooses pancakes. Ann's knowledge on Tuesday did not depend on Friday's actual choice—which had not yet occurred—but on Sam's testimony and reliable pattern. Knowledge of a free choice here rests on pre-choice evidence rather than the actual choice.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W4220703499.c007 fails because knowledge of a free choice can be grounded in pre-choice evidence such as testimony and track record rather than depending on the actual choice itself.

objections.text: Sarah faces a choice at T2: she can help a stranger or walk past. God is eternal, with all moments present to Him, so God perceives Sarah walking past at T2—not as a prediction but as a present, completed reality within His timeless awareness. God's eternal perception is fixed and unalterable; it encompasses the entire timeline as one undivided whole. Now Sarah at T2 deliberates. For libertarian freedom, it must be within Sarah's power to help instead. But if Sarah were to help, God's eternal perception would have included her helping—which it does not. Since God's perception is eternally complete and cannot be otherwise, Sarah cannot do otherwise than what God perceives. The fixity is not removed; it is made permanent. Compare open theism: God knows all real possibilities but not which choice Sarah will make, leaving her future genuinely open. This alternative better respects libertarian freedom, since Sarah's choice remains undetermined by any prior or eternal fact.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c025 fails because positing God as eternal with all time present to Him does not best respect libertarian free will: it merely relocates the fixity of Sarah's choice from temporal foreknowledge to timeless perception, leaving her unable to do otherwise than what God eternally apprehends.

objections.text: Agent S is deliberating at T about whether to raise her arm at T+1. She believes she is free to choose either way, and her choice is not determined by prior causes. However, it is necessarily true that if S will raise her arm at T+1, then she will raise her arm at T+1. This is a trivial internal necessity of the form 'If X then X'. Yet, if God knows at T that S will raise her arm at T+1, then S cannot do otherwise at T+1 without contradicting God’s infallible knowledge, thus undermining her libertarian freedom.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4220703499.c010 fails because even trivial internal necessities like 'If X then X' can conflict with free will when combined with divine foreknowledge.

objections.text: Maria is a surgeon who has settled, over twenty years of practice, that she will never abandon a patient mid-operation. A cardiac arrest occurs. No one coerces her, no drug impels her, no external cause determines her action. She continues the surgery. There was, in effect, only one live option: she could not, given her settled character, genuinely entertain abandonment as a live alternative. No external force closes that option; her own dispositions do. Yet her choice is fully aseity—grounded in herself, uncaused from outside, hers to execute. The premise insists aseity requires that options be open and that it be up to him which option he chooses, implying multiple live alternatives he genuinely picks among. But Maria's self-grounded act occurs with no open alternatives; it is still uncoerced, still her own, still aseity. The premise's condition is stronger than aseity requires.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4220703499.c006 fails because Maria's uncoerced, self-grounded choice with no open alternatives shows that aseity does not require facing multiple open options or picking among them; a settled character can act with full self-grounding from a single viable course.

objections.text: Consider a scenario where an eternal God exists, but human perception of time is relative and dynamic. In this case, a person, Alice, makes a choice that she believes is free, but God's eternal presence means that her choice is already known. However, Alice's understanding of her own freedom is rooted in her experience of time, which is not absolute. If we prioritize Alice's perspective, we see that her choice feels free to her, despite God's foreknowledge.
objections.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it assumes an eternal God's perspective on time must align with human understanding of freedom, which is not necessarily the case.

objections.text: Consider Sarah, a rational agent at T1 who must choose between donating to charity A or B. In a Molinist framework God, outside time, knows the true counterfactuals: if Sarah were to freely choose A, then she would later be satisfied; if she were to freely choose B, she would regret it. God’s middle knowledge fixes the actual world by selecting the counterfactual where Sarah freely chooses A, but this does not require that God sees a static, eternal present of the whole timeline. If instead we posit God’s eternity as a timeless present where the entire history, including Sarah’s choice, is already laid out, Sarah’s decision is no longer open to her; it is simply a point on God’s already‑present timeline, contradicting the Molinist claim that libertarian freedom is preserved by counterfactuals, not by a static eternal view.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W4220703499.c025 fails because Molinism holds that God’s middle knowledge, not an eternal present, secures libertarian freedom, and the eternal‑present view makes choices non‑open.

objections.text: Imagine a man named Elias who chooses to drink water at noon. According to the Grounding Principle, the truth of this choice and the knowledge of it are grounded in Elias's act. If God's knowledge of Elias's choice depends on that contingent act, then God's knowledge is not identical to His necessary essence. Since God is absolutely simple, His knowledge is His being. If His knowledge is grounded in a creature's choice, then God's very existence becomes contingent upon the world, violating divine simplicity and aseity.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4220703499.c007 fails because grounding divine knowledge in contingent creaturely acts contradicts divine simplicity and the necessity of God's essence.

objections.text: Suppose an agent, Clara, is deciding at T1 whether to accept or reject a gift at T2. Because God is eternal and perceives the entire timeline at once, the fact that Clara accepts the gift at T2 is eternally present to Him. Since this fact is eternally true, Clara cannot choose to reject the gift at T2, as doing so would contradict the eternal reality God perceives. Consequently, Clara lacks the open options necessary for libertarian freedom.
objections.premise_fails_because: The eternal fixedness of the timeline precludes the existence of open options, meaning the theory fails to respect libertarian freedom.

objections.text: Consider Mara, a created agent who at noon on a given day freely chooses between two routes, A and B, with nothing in her past or character fixing the outcome. Suppose God, eternal and with all time present to Him, knows at the start of the day that Mara will take route A. Under r1, the Grounding Principle governs only the truth of God's knowledge and its object-side relation to Mara's choice, and any dependence is merely extrinsic. But consider what makes the proposition 'God knows that Mara takes A' true. It is true only because Mara in fact takes A. Had she taken B, God's belief would have been false, so God's knowledge would have been different in content and truth-value. Yet the divine knowing, which r1 treats as necessary and unchanging, now varies with a creaturely choice. The 'extrinsic' label does not remove this: a necessary being whose knowledge-state is counterfactually sensitive to what Mara does is a being whose cognitive profile is contingent on creation, so the essence-level independence r1 claims is not secured by the dependence it admits.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise r1 fails because it asserts that the dependence of God's knowledge on Mara's choice is merely extrinsic and leaves the divine essence uncontingent, yet the counterfactual variation of God's knowledge with Mara's choice shows that this dependence reaches into God's own cognitive profile, so the claim that it does not affect the divine essence does not follow.

objections.text: Consider Sarah at T1, deciding between A (accept a job offer in Lyon) and B (stay in Paris). At T2 she chooses A, and God's eternal perception registers 'Sarah chooses A.' Suppose at T2 Sarah instead deliberates seriously about B and, out of a settled intention formed earlier, would have chosen B had she gone that way. The grounding claim says God's perception is posterior to and grounded in her actual choice, so God's perception of A is fixed only by her choosing A. But the counterfactual 'had she chosen B, God would have perceived B' is then true only if God's perception covaries with her choice, which makes the perception depend on the choice in a way that already makes its content a fact about her options. Whether her choice of A is up to her now depends on whether the perception would have been different, so the unalterability is not merely a consequence of the actual choice: it is the same fixed fact as the one restricting her options. The revised premise assumes posteriority can be separated from the constraint on alternatives, and Sarah's case shows that the separation fails.
objections.premise_fails_because: The premise that God's perception is grounded in and posterior to the choice, yet leaves the choice's alternatives unrestricted, fails because the counterfactual covariation required for grounding makes the perception's unalterability itself constrain which option Sarah can take.

objections.text: At T1, S is a perfectly rational agent who has already, at T0, deliberated exhaustively and formed an unalterable intention to choose A at T2. At T1, S is not choosing but is already settled on A, yet the act of determination (the forming of the intention) occurred at T0. Thus, S has determined between A and B before the moment of choice at T2, contradicting the claim that the determinative act cannot occur before it occurs.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4220703499.arg1.r3 fails because the determinative act can occur before the moment of choice if the agent has already formed an unalterable intention.

restatements.paper_vocabulary: The objection contends that the inference from 'one cannot be choosing before one is choosing' to 'at T1 S cannot choose between A and B' treats 'is choosing' as a prior state that must already obtain, when for a libertarian agent deliberation is the activity by which the choice comes to be; the claim holds only if 'choosing' denotes a completed event, which presupposes the very openness of T1 at issue.
restatements.plain_english: Someone says you can't pick between two options right now, because you can only be in the middle of picking after you've already picked. But when you think something through and then decide, the thinking is the deciding happening. So the claim only sounds right if you assume the decision is already finished, which is the very thing being disputed.
restatements.neighboring_tradition: In the epistemology of disagreement and the debate over doxastic deliberation, this is a charge of question-begging against an argument that assumes the endpoint of a process in order to rule out the process: the inference reads 'deliberating toward a choice' as a completed-event predicate, so it presupposes that the outcome is already settled, which is the point in dispute, and it ignores that the agent's reasoning is itself the process that settles it.

restatements.paper_vocabulary: The objection contends that the truth of, and knowledge about, a future free choice need not be grounded in the choice's actual occurrence (contra the Grounding Principle), since foreknowledge can rest on pre-choice warrant such as the agent's testimony of intention and a reliable track record of follow-through, so that the epistemic and alethic status of the choice is fixed by evidence available prior to the choice rather than by the choice itself.
restatements.plain_english: You can know in advance what someone will freely decide, based on what they told you and how reliably they have kept such promises before, so knowing it doesn't have to depend on the decision actually being made later.
restatements.neighboring_tradition: In the epistemology of testimony and inductive reliabilism, this is a counterexample to a metaphysical grounding claim: predictive knowledge of an agent's future voluntary act is justified by prior testimonial evidence and a reliable behavioural track record, so the knowledge's warrant is not the act itself, and the grounding thesis confuses the evidential basis of the knowledge with its truthmaker.

restatements.paper_vocabulary: The objection contends that positing God's eternal, timeless awareness of all moments as present (the 'eternalist' or 'timeless-knowledge' model) does not respect libertarian freedom: God's eternal perception of Sarah's walking past at T2 is a fixed, complete, unalterable fact, so Sarah at T2 cannot do otherwise, and the fixity is merely made permanent rather than removed. The eternalist solution therefore collapses into a fixity/necessity-of-the-past style argument that transfers the unalterability of God's eternal knowing onto the agent's present power to do otherwise, and the open-theist rival is offered as the better way to preserve the agent's undetermined choice.
restatements.plain_english: God sees everything at once, including what a person will do later. So that view of God's knowing already fixes what the person does. If God's knowledge can't be changed, the person can't really do anything different, so the view doesn't keep the choice free. A rival view, where God knows only what could happen and not which choice will be made, keeps the choice open better.
restatements.neighboring_tradition: In the problem-of-divine-foreknowledge literature, this is a 'fixity of divine knowledge' objection to the eternalist (timeless-knowledge) solution: God's unalterable eternal awareness of the agent's act, like the past in Ockham's argument, is said to render the agent unable to do otherwise, so the eternalist reconciliation fails and an open-theist, limited-foreknowledge alternative is preferred.

rounds.speaker: referee
rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection attacks W4220703499.c007 as stated. The Grounding Principle claims that 'knowledge of a free choice depends upon that actual choice' without restricting whose knowledge is at issue. The objection takes this at face value, applies it to God's knowledge, and argues that the resulting dependency creates theological problems for divine simplicity and aseity. Whether or not this objection succeeds, it engages the premise as written rather than attacking a version the argument does not assert.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You have located a real pressure point, but you have run together two things the Grounding Principle keeps apart. c007 says that the truth of 'Elias drinks at noon' and the knowledge of it are grounded in Elias's act. It does not say that God's essence or existence is grounded in that act. Divine simplicity requires that God's knowledge be identical to His essence; it does not require that the content of His knowledge be necessary in the sense of being fixed independently of what creatures do. The eternalist framing in c025 helps here: if all time is present to God, God's knowing of Elias's choice is a single eternal act whose object is temporal, and the dependence runs from the object to the relation of knowing, not from creation into the divine nature. That is the standard distinction between extrinsic relations of God to creatures and intrinsic changes in God, and it is what lets God be really related to the world without being really changed by it. The argument can be defended on this reading.

But I should be candid that this defence requires making the dependence explicitly extrinsic, and the text does not yet say so. Whether the Grounding Principle can be stated so that it governs only the object-side truth of divine knowledge, without spilling into God's ontological ground, is exactly what the author must spell out. Molina's middle knowledge [W4246671415.a3] faces a parallel worry about the status of God's knowledge prior to the will, and the discussion of whether God's knowledge is a contingent a priori truth [W4403587904.a1] bears on how to separate divine knowing from its contingent objects.
rounds.revised_premise: The Grounding Principle governs only the extrinsic, object-side dependence of the truth and divine knowledge of a free choice on that choice, and does not make God's essence or existence depend on creatures.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
You attempt to rescue the argument by distinguishing between the content of God's knowledge and His essence, labeling the dependence "extrinsic." However, this does not resolve the conflict with divine simplicity. If God’s knowledge is identical to His essence, then any dependence of that knowledge upon a contingent act is necessarily a dependence of His essence. 

By claiming the dependence is merely an "extrinsic relation" to a temporal object, you fail to address how the *truth* of God's knowledge can be grounded in a creature without the essence itself being contingent upon that creature. If the Grounding Principle dictates that the knowledge depends on the choice, and the knowledge *is* the essence, then the essence's truth-condition is tethered to the world. You must explain how an essence can be identical to a state of knowing whose truth-value is determined by a contingent event.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
Your rejoinder is the strongest form of the worry, and I grant its structure: if divine knowing is identical to the divine essence, and that knowing has truth-conditions fixed by a creature's act, then something about the essence is relational to the world. But the step from 'the truth of God's knowledge is grounded in Elias's act' to 'the essence is contingent' equivocates on 'grounded'. Grounding in c007 is a relation between a truth and its ground; it does not make the knower's being depend on the ground. Divine simplicity forbids real composition in God, not real relations to creatures. Aquinas-style accounts treat God's knowing of creatures as a relation of reason on the creature's side and of the object's truth on God's side, which is what makes God really unchanged while the truth of His knowledge is fixed by what occurs [W4246671415.a3 and W2045762660.a2 frame knowledge as prior to and distinct from the will's act, which supports separating the knowing from its contingent object]. The eternalist premise c025 is what keeps this coherent: because all time is present to God, the single eternal knowing has a temporal object without temporal change in the knower. Your question, how an essence can be identical to a knowing whose truth-value is fixed by a contingent event, is answered by saying the truth-value is a fact about the object and the relation, not a further determination of the essence. I concede that the argument as written does not state this; the Grounding Principle needs an explicit extrinsicness clause.

Revised premise: The Grounding Principle governs only the truth of God's knowledge and its object-side relation to the free choice, and any such dependence is an extrinsic relation of God to creatures that does not make the divine essence or existence contingent on creation.

rounds.speaker: referee
rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks W4220703499.c025 as stated. That premise claims positing God as eternal 'best respects both divine foreknowledge and libertarian free will.' The objection argues that God's eternal perception creates permanent fixity that prevents libertarian freedom, and offers open theism as a superior alternative—directly challenging the comparative 'best respects' claim. This is an attack on the premise as stated, however strong or weak, not a misreading.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that God's eternal awareness of Sarah's walking past makes that act settled in the sense that it is perceived as present, but you move too quickly from 'perceived as completed' to 'cannot be otherwise.' The argument's Grounding Principle [W4220703499.c007] says the truth about, and knowledge of, a free choice depends upon the actual choice. On that view God's perception is not an independent cause that fixes Sarah's options; it is the epistemic upshot of what Sarah actually does. If Sarah were to help, the truth about God's awareness would have been different, and that counterfactual dependence is exactly what the Anselmian thesis [W4220703499.c006] requires: open options and it being up to her which one she takes. Your modal step, 'if she helped, God would have included her helping, so she cannot do otherwise,' conflates the fixity of a known truth with the fixity of the act. The literature makes the same move against coercion: God's knowledge of Pilate's act does not coerce it because what is future to Pilate is not future to God [W7202149095.a3]. Your step 'the fixity is made permanent' needs the premise that eternal perception is prior to and independent of the choice, and c027 denies that God's eternal act has the relevant priority in the way you need [W4220703499.c027]. Open theism is a live alternative, but it has its own cost (God does not know which choice will be made), and the objection does not show that the eternal-presence model is worse on respecting freedom. I concede that the argument's support for the eternal model depends on the Grounding Principle being accepted as explaining why God's perception is non-coercive; without it, the objection has real force.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: Your Grounding Principle establishes counterfactual dependence: had Sarah helped, God's awareness would differ. But counterfactual dependence doesn't show open options. The principle explains why God perceives what He does — it tracks the actual choice — yet it presupposes that one choice is actual, not that both remain available at T2. You concede God's perception is eternally unalterable. At T2, God perceives walking past as completed reality, and that cannot be otherwise. You say the perception isn't prior to or independent of the choice, and I accept that. But you still owe an explanation of why an eternally unalterable perception of one outcome leaves both options genuinely open. The Grounding Principle removes causal priority; it does not remove the modal fixity that, for the libertarian, is the real threat.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that I owe more than counterfactual dependence. Counterfactual dependence shows that God's perception tracks Sarah's actual choice, but you are correct that it does not by itself show that both options are open at T2. Your strongest point is the modal one: if God's perception of walking past is eternally unalterable, then at T2 Sarah seems unable to make God's perception otherwise, and that looks like a fixity the libertarian must reject. My reply is that unalterability is a property of a truth about a choice, not a constraint on the choice, and the Anselmian thesis [W4220703499.c006] needs only that it be up to Sarah which option she takes. Pilate's case makes the same distinction: what is future to Pilate is not future to God, so God's knowledge does not coerce the act [W7202149095.a3]. But this reply works only if the eternal perception is not the kind of fixed prior fact that settles the choice, and nothing in the argument has yet shown that. The grounding of the perception in the choice (c007) is what does that work, and you have correctly noted it does not establish open options by itself. So the argument needs one further premise.

Revised premise: God's eternal perception of Sarah's choice is grounded in, and logically posterior to, the choice itself, so that its unalterability is a consequence of the actual choice and does not restrict which option Sarah can take at T2.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content: You assume that because God's eternal perception is complete and unalterable, it removes Sarah's power to do otherwise. But the argument does not claim that God's knowledge floats free of her act; rather, the truth about her choice and God's knowledge of it depend upon that very choice [W4220703499.c007]. What you call fixity is merely the internal necessity that if God eternally perceives Sarah walking past, then she walks past, and the argument explicitly denies that such internal necessity conflicts with libertarian freedom [W4220703499.c010]. From Sarah's standpoint at T2, her future remains open: what is future to her is not future to God, so His eternal knowledge does not coerce her temporal act [W7202131248.a3]. Within God's single eternal act we can still distinguish what is logically prior and subsequent [W4220703499.c027], so His knowledge follows from—rather than dictates—her free decision. Your open-theist alternative is not the only way to leave Sarah's future open; on this eternalist picture, her choice at T2 is genuinely up to her [W4220703499.c006], and God's timeless awareness is the consequence, not the cause, of that choice.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You invoke the Grounding Principle: God's knowledge depends on Sarah's choice, so His knowledge follows from rather than dictates her act. But grounding is about explanation, not modal power. The question is whether Sarah can do otherwise given that God's eternal perception is fixed. You accept that God's perception is unalterable and that if God perceives Sarah walking past, she walks past. So: God's perception is necessarily what it is, and it necessarily entails Sarah's act. The conclusion—that Sarah necessarily walks past—follows regardless of which direction the grounding runs. Calling this "internal necessity" mischaracterizes it. "If X then X" constrains nothing; "If God perceives P, then P," combined with God's perception being eternally fixed, constrains Sarah. Your counterfactual—"if she chose differently, God would perceive differently"—requires Sarah to have the power to make God's eternal perception otherwise than it eternally is. That is precisely what eternal fixity denies.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
Even so, you are right that grounding is not modality and that 'If X then X' [W4220703499.c010] does not by itself cover the entailment from a fixed eternal perception. The argument must explicitly add that God's eternal perception, though immutable within any single world, is contingent across possible worlds on the creature's free choice. Sarah's power to do otherwise is not a power to change what God eternally knows in the actual world; it is a power to actualize a different world in which God's eternal knowledge was always of her helping. Because the creature's act is logically prior within God's eternal act [W4220703499.c027], the content of that act varies with the creature's choice without any change in God. What is future to Sarah is not future to God, so His eternal knowledge does not coerce her temporal act [W7202131248.a3]. Your challenge shows that without an explicit contingency premise, the argument risks collapsing into fatalism.

Revised premise: God's eternal perception, though immutable within any given possible world, is contingent on the creature's free choice across possible worlds, so its fixity within a world does not entail that the creature cannot do otherwise.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: Your Maya case shows that deliberation is an activity that unfolds over time, and I grant that. But c019 does not say deliberation cannot occur before the choice is complete; it says that S cannot already be in the state of choosing A rather than B at T1 while also being open to the alternative. Deliberation at T1 is compatible with that: Maya weighs reasons and rejects B, and what the argument needs is that the settling of the option is not yet fixed at T1. Your phrase 'the activity that makes the choice occur' actually supports the Anselmian thesis in [W4220703499.c006]: the agent's choosing must be up to him and not already determined, so the option is open until the activity concludes. The worry is whether the ten seconds are 'idle' if the outcome is already settled, and that is the point the Grounding Principle [W4220703499.c007] addresses: the truth about the choice depends on the actual choice, so the fact that A was chosen does not precede the choosing. I concede that c019 as worded is ambiguous between 'not yet choosing' and 'not yet settled', and that the inference from the first to the second is not secured by the premise. The argument survives only if we read c019 as the claim that the outcome is not yet fixed while deliberation proceeds, which is what c006 requires.
rounds.revised_premise: At T1 S's choice between A and B is not yet settled, since the deliberative activity that would settle it is still in progress and has not determined its outcome.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
The concession is useful, but it does not yet secure c019. You now say c019 means only that "the outcome is not yet fixed while deliberation proceeds." That reading is not what c019 states. c019 claims that at T1 S "cannot choose between A and B" because he "cannot be choosing before he is choosing." The reason given is about the activity of choosing, and that is the step Maya's case attacks. An open outcome is a different claim from an incapacity to choose, and the argument needs the second to follow from the first.

The reformulated reading also faces a dilemma. If the outcome is open at T1, then c019 is not needed, because openness is already what c006 requires. If the outcome is already fixed at T1 by God's eternal perception, which c007 and the r2 revision make posterior to the choice, then the ten seconds are settled before they run, and the open-options condition in c006 fails. The Grounding Principle cannot both leave the outcome open at T1 and let the choice be grounded in an eternal perception that is already there. You need to say which horn you take.

Finally, r2 asserts that God's perception is logically posterior to the choice, yet the argument's conclusion concerns God's eternal knowledge, which is supposed to be prior to every choice. Until that tension is resolved, the defence has not shown that the open-options premise survives.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that c019 as worded states an incapacity, and my previous reading shifted it to 'the outcome is not yet fixed.' I will not keep that shift. Your Maya case does show that 'is choosing' names an ongoing activity, not a completed event, so the step from 'cannot be choosing before choosing' to 'cannot choose between A and B at T1' does not go through. Deliberation at T1 is a choosing between A and B, and Maya's case gives no reason to think it is excluded. Your dilemma is also sound against the r2 version. If God's perception is grounded in the choice and the choice is settled at T1, the open-options condition in [W4220703499.c006] fails. The Grounding Principle [W4220703499.c007] cannot both leave the outcome open at T1 and make the truth about it depend on an eternal perception already in place. The two horns are not reconciled by the posteriority claim, because that claim concerns what grounds God's knowledge, while the conclusion needs God's knowledge to be prior to the choice. objection.text: Consider Maya, a chess player at T1 who is weighing two moves, A (Nf3) and B (d4). She deliberates for ten seconds, then plays A. Her premise is that she is choosing now, while the options are open. Suppose a rival says: 'At T1 you cannot choose between A and B, since choosing is something you can only be doing after you have chosen.' Test this against Maya's case. Her deliberation is itself the process of choosing: weighing reasons, rejecting B, settling on A. Nothing in that process requires the choice to be complete before it begins. If choosing could occur only after it had finished, no one could ever deliberate toward a decision, and Maya's ten seconds would be idle. The inference treats 'is choosing' as a state that must already hold, when for a free agent it is the activity that makes the choice occur. The claim that one cannot be choosing before one is choosing is true only if 'choosing' names a completed event, which begs the question about whether T1 is open.

objection.text: Sarah faces a choice at T2: she can help a stranger or walk past. God is eternal, with all moments present to Him, so God perceives Sarah walking past at T2—not as a prediction but as a present, completed reality within His timeless awareness. God's eternal perception is fixed and unalterable; it encompasses the entire timeline as one undivided whole. Now Sarah at T2 deliberates. For libertarian freedom, it must be within Sarah's power to help instead. But if Sarah were to help, God's eternal perception would have included her helping—which it does not. Since God's perception is eternally complete and cannot be otherwise, Sarah cannot do otherwise than what God perceives. The fixity is not removed; it is made permanent. Compare open theism: God knows all real possibilities but not which choice Sarah will make, leaving her future genuinely open. This alternative better respects libertarian freedom, since Sarah's choice remains undetermined by any prior or eternal fact.

objection.text: Agent S is deliberating at T about whether to raise her arm at T+1. She believes she is free to choose either way, and her choice is not determined by prior causes. objection.premise_fails_because: W4220703499.c010 fails because even trivial internal necessities like 'If X then X' can conflict with free will when combined with divine foreknowledge.

objection.text: Maria is a surgeon who has settled, over twenty years of practice, that she will never abandon a patient mid-operation. A cardiac arrest occurs. No one coerces her, no drug impels her, no external cause determines her action. She continues the surgery. No external force closes that option; her own dispositions do. Yet her choice is fully aseity—grounded in herself, uncaused from outside, hers to execute. The premise insists aseity requires that options be open and that it be up to him which option he chooses, implying multiple live alternatives he genuinely picks among. That premise claims positing God as eternal 'best respects both divine foreknowledge and libertarian free will.' turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You have located a real pressure point, but you have run together two things the Grounding Principle keeps apart. c007 says that the truth of 'Elias drinks at noon' and the knowledge of it are grounded in Elias's act. It does not say that God's essence or existence is grounded in that act. Divine simplicity requires that God's knowledge be identical to His essence; it does not require that the content of His knowledge be necessary in the sense of being fixed independently of what creatures do. The eternalist framing in c025 helps here: if all time is present to God, God's knowing of Elias's choice is a single eternal act whose object is temporal, and the dependence runs from the object to the relation of knowing, not from creation into the divine nature. That is the standard distinction between extrinsic relations of God to creatures and intrinsic changes in God, and it is what lets God be really related to the world without being really changed by it. The argument can be defended on this reading.

But I should be candid that this defence requires making the dependence explicitly extrinsic, and the text does not yet say so. Whether the Grounding Principle can be stated so that it governs only the object-side truth of divine knowledge, without spilling into God's ontological ground, is exactly what the author must spell out. Molina's middle knowledge [W4246671415.a3] faces a parallel worry about the status of God's knowledge prior to the will, and the discussion of whether God's knowledge is a contingent a priori truth [W4403587904.a1] bears on how to separate divine knowing from its contingent objects.
turn.revised_premise: The Grounding Principle governs only the extrinsic, object-side dependence of the truth and divine knowledge of a free choice on that choice, and does not make God's essence or existence depend on creatures.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content: You are right that God's eternal awareness of Sarah's walking past makes that act settled in the sense that it is perceived as present, but you move too quickly from 'perceived as completed' to 'cannot be otherwise.' The argument's Grounding Principle [W4220703499.c007] says the truth about, and knowledge of, a free choice depends upon the actual choice. On that view God's perception is not an independent cause that fixes Sarah's options; it is the epistemic upshot of what Sarah actually does. If Sarah were to help, the truth about God's awareness would have been different, and that counterfactual dependence is exactly what the Anselmian thesis [W4220703499.c006] requires: open options and it being up to her which one she takes. Your modal step, 'if she helped, God would have included her helping, so she cannot do otherwise,' conflates the fixity of a known truth with the fixity of the act. The literature makes the same move against coercion: God's knowledge of Pilate's act does not coerce it because what is future to Pilate is not future to God [W7202149095.a3]. Your step 'the fixity is made permanent' needs the premise that eternal perception is prior to and independent of the choice, and c027 denies that God's eternal act has the relevant priority in the way you need [W4220703499.c027]. Open theism is a live alternative, but it has its own cost (God does not know which choice will be made), and the objection does not show that the eternal-presence model is worse on respecting freedom. I concede that the argument's support for the eternal model depends on the Grounding Principle being accepted as explaining why God's perception is non-coercive; without it, the objection has real force.

You attempt to rescue the argument by distinguishing between the content of God's knowledge and His essence, labeling the dependence "extrinsic." However, this does not resolve the conflict with divine simplicity. If God’s knowledge is identical to His essence, then any dependence of that knowledge upon a contingent act is necessarily a dependence of His essence. 

By claiming the dependence is merely an "extrinsic relation" to a temporal object, you fail to address how the *truth* of God's knowledge can be grounded in a creature without the essence itself being contingent upon that creature. If the Grounding Principle dictates that the knowledge depends on the choice, and the knowledge *is* the essence, then the essence's truth-condition is tethered to the world. You must explain how an essence can be identical to a state of knowing whose truth-value is determined by a contingent event.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
Your rejoinder is the strongest form of the worry, and I grant its structure: if divine knowing is identical to the divine essence, and that knowing has truth-conditions fixed by a creature's act, then something about the essence is relational to the world. But the step from 'the truth of God's knowledge is grounded in Elias's act' to 'the essence is contingent' equivocates on 'grounded'. Grounding in c007 is a relation between a truth and its ground; it does not make the knower's being depend on the ground. Divine simplicity forbids real composition in God, not real relations to creatures. Aquinas-style accounts treat God's knowing of creatures as a relation of reason on the creature's side and of the object's truth on God's side, which is what makes God really unchanged while the truth of His knowledge is fixed by what occurs [W4246671415.a3 and W2045762660.a2 frame knowledge as prior to and distinct from the will's act, which supports separating the knowing from its contingent object]. The eternalist premise c025 is what keeps this coherent: because all time is present to God, the single eternal knowing has a temporal object without temporal change in the knower. Your question, how an essence can be identical to a knowing whose truth-value is fixed by a contingent event, is answered by saying the truth-value is a fact about the object and the relation, not a further determination of the essence. I concede that the argument as written does not state this; the Grounding Principle needs an explicit extrinsicness clause.

The principle explains why God perceives what He does — it tracks the actual choice — yet it presupposes that one choice is actual, not that both remain available at T2. My reply is that unalterability is a property of a truth about a choice, not a constraint on the choice, and the Anselmian thesis [W4220703499.c006] needs only that it be up to Sarah which option she takes. Pilate's case makes the same distinction: what is future to Pilate is not future to God, so God's knowledge does not coerce the act [W7202149095.a3]. Within God's single eternal act we can still distinguish what is logically prior and subsequent [W4220703499.c027], so His knowledge follows from—rather than dictates—her free decision. Your open-theist alternative is not the only way to leave Sarah's future open; on this eternalist picture, her choice at T2 is genuinely up to her [W4220703499.c006], and God's timeless awareness is the consequence, not the cause, of that choice.

Your counterfactual—"if she chose differently, God would perceive differently"—requires Sarah to have the power to make God's eternal perception otherwise than it eternally is.
